newsitem.title: FRANCE: Disposal of arms plutonium to take decades - experts.
newsitem.headline: Disposal of arms plutonium to take decades - experts.

text.p: Nuclear safety experts debating how to get rid of plutonium from scrapped Russian and U.S. nuclear weapons concluded on Thursday the task was feasible but would take decades.

"The problem can be solved. That's the main message we're passing on to our governments," said Claude Mandil, a senior French Industry Ministry official who chaired the four-day conference in Paris of experts from 10 nations.

"It will need years of work to eliminate the last gram of this stock," he told a news conference after the talks involving the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial democracies, together with Russia, Belgium, Switzerland and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

Recommendations from the experts, could pave the way to decisions by G7 nations at a summit in Denver, Colorado, in June 1997. The G7 comprises the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada.
Mandil said there was no clear best way of disposing of the highly poisonous plutonium, one of the most disturbing legacies of the Cold War, and that a variety of techniques was likely to be used.
The only option experts ruled out was merely to drill deep holes to bury the material, reckoning it insufficiently secure.

Among the possible methods of disposal was to burn the plutonium in special nuclear reactors to create civilian electricity. The process involves blending plutonium and uranium into a fuel called MOX (mixed oxide) fuel.
Russia is cooperating with France and Germany over a factory to produce MOX at Mayak in the Urals. Mandil said the plant should be completed within five years.

Another possibiilty is to seal the plutonium in glass by a process of vitrification preventing the plutonium from being extracted for later military use. Mandil said the United States said the technology was within its reach.

"It's probable that all (options) will be needed because the quantities are so large," he said. He said the United States and Russia each had about 50 tonnes of plutonium from weapons due to be dismantled under arms control accords.
"It will take time, which means that an intermediate stockage will be necessary," he said.

Nikolai Yegorov, a deputy Russian Atomic Energy Minister who headed Moscow's delegation, said a single plant would suffice to process plutonium in Russia into MOX fuel. But Russia would then have to build several special reactors to burn the fuel.
The international environmental group Greenpeace expressed concern about the plans to use plutonium to generate electricity, saying reprocessing was a main source of radioactive pollution.
